bookCover.coverDescription:
Ethical Analysis Skills & the Ethical Toolbox

A BriGRETE module on moral argumentation and normative ethical theory

params.alt: BriGRETE module cover: Ethical Analysis Skills and the Ethical Toolbox.
Title slide: Ethical Analysis Skills and the Ethical Toolbox, a BriGRETE module.

params.text:
Welcome to the Ethical Toolbox

Institutional research ethics cannot rest on the high-stakes guesswork of personal intuition. Intuition is unstable: it varies from person to person and rarely supplies the universal criteria that rigorous oversight demands. This module replaces gut feeling with an engineered architecture of verifiable reasoning — a logical pipeline that moves from the mechanics of language, through the formal structure of argument, to the normative theories we use to resolve real dilemmas.

The system works in three stages, and the order matters. Skipping the linguistic foundation lets logical fallacies slip in and quietly compromise the final decision.

Precise language is the load-bearing foundation. Many apparent moral disagreements are really unrecognised linguistic misunderstandings that dissolve once terms are clearly defined and ambiguity and vagueness are audited out.

Once language is clean, facts can be assembled into formally structured arguments. Here we distinguish validity from soundness, recognise deductive forms, and learn why no pile of facts can cross the gap to an ‘ought’ on its own.
Deontology, utilitarianism and virtue ethics supply the evaluative premises that bridge the is–ought gap, giving reviewers a defensible source for their value judgements.

Who this is for & what you will gain

This module is designed for Research Ethics Committee (REC) members supervising projects and specialised ethics questions (AI, digital data), and for researchers who need foundational knowledge to engage in active ethical debate. By the end you will be able to:

  • Diagnose linguistic sources of moral disagreement (definitions, ambiguity, vagueness).
  • Assess arguments for validity and soundness and identify common fallacies.
  • Distinguish factual from evaluative claims and spot the is–ought fallacy.
  • Apply deontological, utilitarian and virtue-based frameworks to research dilemmas.
  • Reason about personhood, moral status and the boundaries of the moral community.

Estimated duration: 75–90 minutes.

params.alt: Three pillars labelled Definitions, Ambiguity and Vagueness supporting a beam that reads: clear language is the foundation of moral argumentation.

params.text:
Language is the load-bearing wall

Clear language is the foundation of all moral argumentation. Disagreements often stem from linguistic misunderstandings rather than genuine moral difference. This section audits three pillars that keep the structure sound: how we define terms, how we detect ambiguity, and how we manage vagueness. Getting these right sanitises our claims before they ever enter the logical-deduction phase of a review.

params.alt: Diagram: Definiendum (the term to be defined) linked to Definiens (the term used to define). Below, Extension (the objects a term applies to) versus Intension (the properties attributed to the term).

params.text:
The parts of a definition

Every definition has two roles. The definiendum is the term being defined; the definiens is the expression that does the defining. A definition works well only when it captures both dimensions of a term's meaning.

  • Extension — the set of all objects the term actually applies to (e.g. every red thing, for ‘red’).
  • Intension — the properties or conceptual meaning we attribute to the term (e.g. water being colourless and odourless).

Relying on extension alone, without pinning down the required intension, creates systemic vulnerabilities in research guidelines: two people can point at the same examples while meaning quite different things.

params.alt: Table of three definition types: Lexical (reports usual meaning), Stipulative (introduces new meanings or abbreviations), Precising (adds specific boundaries for practical rules).

params.text:
Choosing the right kind of definition

Not all definitions do the same job. Matching the type to the task keeps analysis honest.

  • Lexical — reports how a term is ordinarily used, as a dictionary does.
  • Stipulative — assigns a new, strict meaning to a term for a specific task, such as coining a unique institutional review code (e.g. ‘20REC’).
  • Precising — tightens the fuzzy boundaries of an existing term for a practical rule, e.g. defining a ‘child’ specifically as someone under 13.

Watch for pitfalls: circularity (using the definiendum inside the definiens) and persuasive definitions that smuggle in emotional connotations.

params.alt: Two-sided diagram: Ambiguity (multiple distinct meanings: lexical, structural, referential) versus Vagueness (imprecise, fuzzy boundaries such as tall or old). Footer defines the equivocation fallacy.

params.text:
Two different failures of clarity

Ambiguity is having multiple distinct meanings. It comes in three forms: lexical (one word, several meanings), structural/syntactic (the grammar allows more than one reading), and referential (it is unclear which entity a pronoun points to).

Vagueness is different in kind: a single meaning with fuzzy boundaries, where it is unclear whether an object falls under the term. Words like ‘tall’ or ‘old’ have no exact numerical cut-off. In weak research proposals, vague language often hides errors in the underlying moral reasoning.

The equivocation fallacy occurs when an argument subtly shifts the meaning of an ambiguous term between a premise and the conclusion — which makes the argument invalid.

params.alt: Building-block diagram: two premises (reasons) supporting a conclusion (supported claim). Linguistic indicators listed: premises use because, since, given that; conclusions use thus, therefore, hence.

params.text:
From clean language to structured reasoning

In this technical sense an argument is a rigid structure in which premises provide explicit reasons for believing a conclusion. Spotting the parts is easier with linguistic indicators:

  • Premise indicators: because, since, given that, for.
  • Conclusion indicators: thus, therefore, hence.

With language sanitised in Section 1, we can now assess how well premises support conclusions.

params.alt: Two nested circles: the inner circle Validity (focus: logical structure; if premises are true the conclusion must be true) sits inside the larger circle Soundness (focus: reality; the argument is valid AND premises are actually true).

params.text:
Structure first, truth second

Validity is about logical structure alone: an argument is valid if it is impossible for the premises to be true while the conclusion is false (truth-preservation). Crucially, an argument can be valid even when its premises are factually false — think of ‘the moon is made of cheese’ reasoning that still flows correctly.

Soundness is stronger: an argument is sound if it is valid and all its premises are actually true. Soundness is what connects the logic to reality.

params.alt: Five boxes showing deductive forms: Modus Ponens, Modus Tollens, Disjunctive Syllogism, Hypothetical Syllogism, Simple Constructive Dilemma, each with its symbolic pattern.

params.text:
Recognising valid patterns

Several deductive forms are reliably valid. Learning to recognise them speeds up review and helps you see when an argument merely imitates a valid shape.
If A then B. A. Therefore B. — affirming the antecedent.
If A then B. Not B. Therefore not A. — denying the consequent.
A or B. Not A. Therefore B.
If A then B. If B then C. Therefore if A then C. — chaining conditionals.
A or B. If A then C. If B then C. Therefore C.

params.alt: Balance-scale diagram comparing a target entity with a known comparative entity, with three evaluation criteria: number of shared properties, diversity of shared properties, and (crucially) relevance of properties to the conclusion.

params.text:
Reasoning from similar cases

An argument from analogy runs: A is similar to B; A has property C; therefore B has property C. These arguments are not deductively valid, but they can be more or less plausible. Three factors strengthen them:

  1. Number of relevant shared properties.
  2. Diversity of those shared properties.
  3. Relevance of the shared properties to the conclusion — the crucial factor.

Peter Singer's drowning child analogy in ‘Famine, Affluence, and Morality’ argues that if we would save a child drowning in front of us at small cost, we are similarly obligated to donate to save distant lives. You will test this analogy in the Case Lab.

answers.text: It makes the similarity more robust, so the conclusion is more likely to hold.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Diverse shared features reduce the chance the analogy rests on a coincidence.
Analogical arguments remain non-deductive regardless of diversity.
Diversity does not address the fact/value gap.

answers.text: It converts a thin term into a thick term.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Unrelated to analogical strength.

params.alt: Split diagram: Factual statements describe how things ARE; Evaluative statements express how things OUGHT TO BE. A spectrum contrasts thin terms (purely evaluative: right, wrong) with thick terms (descriptive + evaluative: courage).

params.text:
Is versus ought — and the terms that carry value

Factual (descriptive) statements describe states of affairs — how things are. Evaluative (normative) statements express value or obligation — how things ought to be. The words we use sit on a spectrum:

  • Thin terms (e.g. right, wrong, good, bad) are purely evaluative.
  • Thick terms (e.g. courage, cruelty) carry both a descriptive component and an evaluative judgement.

Identifying whether a premise is factual or evaluative determines the logical limits of the argument it can support — which sets up the central crisis of moral logic in the next chapter.

params.alt: Staircase diagram of moral categories from bottom to top: Forbidden (impermissible), Permissible (morally indifferent), Obligatory (mandatory), Supererogatory (admirable, above and beyond).

params.text:
How strongly does morality bind an action?

Evaluative language sorts actions into a hierarchy of moral demand:

  • Forbidden — impermissible; must not be done.
  • Permissible — morally indifferent; neither required nor forbidden.
  • Obligatory — mandatory (morally or legally); not doing it is impermissible.
  • Supererogatory — admirable and praiseworthy but not required — going above and beyond.

An action is a moral obligation precisely when it is not permissible not to perform it. Supererogatory acts sit above obligation: good to do, but no one is blamed for omitting them.

params.alt: A broken bridge over a chasm: on the left, Factual Premises (What IS); on the right, Evaluative Conclusion (What OUGHT to be). The missing keystone is labelled 'An Evaluative Premise'. Caption: every valid moral argument needs at least one evaluative premise to cross the gap.

params.text:
The central crisis of moral logic

The broken bridge pictures the core problem: trying to derive a moral ought purely from factual is premises. The left cliff is empirical data (what is); the right cliff is the ethical conclusion (what ought to be). The gap between them is the is–ought fallacy.

No amount of factual data — however precise or voluminous — can cross this gap by itself. The missing keystone is an evaluative premise: every valid moral argument needs at least one. Without it, research data stays morally inert and cannot dictate action. This is exactly why we need normative theories — a reliable source for that evaluative premise.

params.alt: Three open doorways labelled Deontologism (Rules & Duties), Utilitarianism (Consequences) and Virtue Ethics (Character). Caption: when moral intuitions conflict, we rely on structured normative frameworks to decide the truth value of our evaluative premises.

params.text:
Where do evaluative premises come from?

If every valid moral argument needs an evaluative premise, we must source it responsibly — not from raw intuition, but from structured normative frameworks. Three dominant families each answer ‘what makes an action right?’ differently:

  • Deontologism — rules and duties; the rightness of the act itself.
  • Utilitarianism — consequences; the outcomes for everyone affected.
  • Virtue ethics — the character of the moral agent.

These frameworks provide the load-bearing premises that let us cross the is–ought chasm and legitimise institutional conclusions.

params.alt: A 2x2 matrix of duties. Columns: Perfect Duties (must abide in all circumstances) and Imperfect Duties (agent chooses when to abide). Rows: Role-Based (inherited by profession/status, e.g. researchers) and Universal (applies to all rational agents).

params.text:
Rules and duties, not outcomes

Deontologism evaluates actions by rules and duties rather than results. Duties can be mapped on two axes:

  • Perfect duties must be abided by in all circumstances (e.g. do not fabricate data); imperfect duties leave the agent latitude over how and when to fulfil them (e.g. help others).
  • Role-based duties are inherited from a profession or status (researchers, REC members); universal duties apply to all rational agents.

W.D. Ross added the idea of prima facie obligations — genuine duties such as fidelity, reparation, gratitude, beneficence and nonmaleficence that can be outweighed by one another in a given situation.

params.alt: Two panels: the Universalizability Principle (act only on maxims you can will to become universal law without logical contradiction) and the Respect for Persons Principle (treat all persons as ends in themselves, never merely as a means).

params.text:
Two tests for a maxim

A maxim is the subjective principle guiding your action. Kant offers two tests:

  • Universalizability: act only on maxims you could will to become a universal law without logical contradiction. Could ‘everyone fabricates data when convenient’ be universalised? No — it would destroy the very trust that makes data meaningful.
  • Respect for Persons: treat all persons as ends in themselves, never merely as a means. Using someone purely as an instrument — ignoring their autonomy and intrinsic value — violates this principle.

Kant also distinguishes direct duties (owed to persons) from indirect duties (actions regarding non-persons that ultimately affect persons).

params.alt: Concentric-circle target diagram of moral status: outer ring Sentience (capacity to feel pain/pleasure), middle ring Grounding Capacities (rationality, ability to have interests, empathy), inner core Full Moral Status / Personhood (maximum rights, intrinsic value, inviolability).

params.text:
Who counts, and why?

To have moral status is to matter for one's own sake — to possess intrinsic rather than merely instrumental value. The diagram layers the debate:

  • Sentience — the fundamental capacity to feel pleasure and pain; often proposed as the threshold for entering the moral circle.
  • Grounding capacities — rationality, the ability to have interests, empathy.
  • Full moral status / personhood — the maximal set of rights, intrinsic value and inviolability.

The distinction between intrinsic value (valuable for its own sake) and instrumental value (valuable as a means) runs through the whole debate — and reappears when we ask about animals, AI and enhanced beings in the Case Lab.

params.alt: Equation-style diagram: the Consequentialist Thesis (rightness depends on expected consequences for everyone affected) PLUS the Axiological Thesis (defining what is valuable: hedonism/pleasure or preference satisfaction) EQUALS Classic Utilitarianism.

params.text:
Two theses combine into one theory

Utilitarianism shifts the focus entirely onto outcomes. Classic utilitarianism is the sum of two claims:

  • Consequentialist thesis — the rightness of an action depends solely on its consequences for everyone affected.
  • Axiological thesis — a theory of what makes a consequence valuable. Classic versions adopt hedonism (pleasure is the only intrinsic good, pain the only intrinsic bad) or preference satisfaction.

Robert Nozick's Experience Machine challenges hedonism: if a machine could give you perfectly pleasant experiences, would you plug in for life? Most say no — suggesting we value being in touch with reality and our own agency, not just felt pleasure.

params.alt: Two flow diagrams: Act-Utilitarianism (evaluate the specific action, calculate utility for all, do the act that maximises utility) versus Rule-Utilitarianism (evaluate the rule, ask whether general adherence maximises utility, ensure the action aligns with the maximising rule).

params.text:
Maximise the act, or maximise the rule?

Act-utilitarianism evaluates each specific action: calculate the utility for all affected and do whatever maximises it. Rule-utilitarianism evaluates the rule: choose actions that follow a rule which, if generally adopted, would maximise utility.

The difference bites in the Trolley Dilemma. An act-utilitarian typically pulls the switch — one death instead of five maximises total utility. A rule-utilitarian may resist, reasoning that a society-wide rule making individuals disposable for the majority could reduce overall utility in the long run.

params.alt: A number line with the Vice of Deficiency (e.g. cowardice) on the left, the Vice of Excess (e.g. recklessness) on the right, and Virtue / the Golden Mean (e.g. courage) at the centre. Caption: focus shifts from actions to character traits, evaluated through moral exemplars.

params.text:
Character rather than acts or outcomes

Virtue ethics evaluates the character of the moral agent rather than isolated actions or their consequences. Virtues are trained, excellent traits — integrity, courage, autonomy.

Aristotle's Doctrine of the Mean places each virtue between two vices: courage is the mean between cowardice (deficiency) and recklessness (excess). Right action is judged by what a moral exemplar — a person of genuinely good character — would do.

params.text:
Putting the toolbox to work

Testing an ethical framework requires high-pressure scenarios that push our moral intuitions to their breaking point. In this Case Lab you will run seven challenges through the tools from Sections 1–3. Each chapter pairs the case slide with a short walkthrough video and a discussion prompt. There are no single ‘correct’ answers — the goal is disciplined analysis.

params.alt: Case Lab slide comparing Singer's Pond (saving a toddler drowning in knee-deep water, mapped to donating small amounts to charity) with Thomson's Violinist (being plugged into an unconscious violinist for nine months, mapped to bodily autonomy and abortion rights).

params.text:
Where does an analogy hold — and where does it break?

Singer's Pond: if you would ruin expensive shoes to save a drowning toddler, the personal cost is minor and the benefit is a life — so, Singer argues, you are similarly obligated to donate to save distant lives. Thomson's Violinist: you wake up medically connected to an unconscious violinist; unplugging reclaims your bodily autonomy but ends his life, pitting bodily freedom against preserving another.

Discussion: Identify the similarities and, crucially, the dissimilarities. Using the three criteria (number, diversity, relevance of shared properties), what makes each analogy strong or weak? Finding where an analogy fails clarifies our core priorities.

params.alt: Case Lab slide: The Art Robot (a robot identifies a pixel is factually yellow but cannot judge beauty without a normative rule) alongside The Homework Lie (1: lying is wrong - evaluative; 2: saying you did homework when you didn't is lying - factual; 3: therefore it is wrong - evaluative).

params.text:
Separating observation from judgement

The Art Robot can determine that a pixel is factually yellow — an empirical observation — but cannot conclude the painting is beautiful without a programmed normative rule. The Homework Lie shows a valid moral argument working correctly: it reaches an evaluative conclusion only because it includes an evaluative premise (‘lying is wrong’) alongside the factual one.

Discussion: Where exactly does each argument move from ‘is’ to ‘ought’? Conflating raw data with moral judgement creates a flawed foundation whose conclusions lack logical integrity.

params.alt: Case Lab slide: a crossed-out balance scale rejecting the weighing of fabricated data against useful results. Prompt 1: apply the Universalizability Principle. Prompt 2: apply the Respect for Persons Principle (e.g. simplifying low-literacy consent).

params.text:
Duty is absolute — outcomes do not decide

Deontology rejects weighing an action against its outcomes (the crossed-out scale). Test the cases against Kant's two principles:

  • Prompt 1 (Universalizability): could ‘fabricate data when convenient’ be a universal law? No — it would destroy scientific reliability, so it is forbidden.
  • Prompt 2 (Respect for Persons): does simplifying a consent form for a low-literacy population respect participants as autonomous agents, or use them merely as means? Consider whether the simplification preserves genuine understanding and choice.

Discussion: These rigid rules ensure the drive for scientific progress does not bypass individual rights.

params.text:
Calculating the greatest good

The Experience Machine tests hedonism: if a tank offered perfect simulated happiness, would you plug in for life? The Trolley Dilemma tests consequentialism: a runaway train heads for five people and you can divert it to a track with one.

Discussion: Contrast the act-utilitarian response (pull the switch: one death maximises utility) with the rule-utilitarian worry (a society-wide rule that makes individuals disposable may lower overall utility).

params.alt: Case Lab slide: Case 1 Data Sharing - an imperfectly anonymised patient dataset could enable fast, cheap medical AI diagnosis; analyse act vs rule evaluation of privacy risks vs global health benefits. Case 2 Grant Review - Proposal A (10,000 people, certain local benefit) vs Proposal B (global breakthrough, highly uncertain); analyse expected utility with unknown variables.

params.text:
Cold mathematics, complex human lives

Research Ethics Committees carry the utilitarian burden of balancing competing harms and benefits across populations.

  • Case 1 — Data Sharing: an imperfectly anonymised dataset risks patient privacy but could train an AI for global diagnoses. Weigh the act-level privacy risk against the rule-level and long-term health benefits.
  • Case 2 — Grant Review: Proposal A guarantees benefit for 10,000 people; Proposal B chases a massive but highly uncertain breakthrough. How do you assign a numerical value to a possible global cure?

Discussion: Expected-utility reasoning forces us to turn uncertainty into calculated action — and to be honest about what the numbers cannot capture.

metadata.title: Case Lab: boundaries of moral status

params.text:
When the subjects are not (ordinary) humans

As laboratories generate new categories of existence, our definition of personhood must adapt to prevent new forms of systemic harm.

  • AI Sentience: design a Turing-style test for machine consciousness. What specific criteria — sentience? rationality? the capacity for interests? — would confer moral status on an AI?
  • Supra-Persons: if rights are tied to human capacities, what happens when bioengineered beings exceed our cognition? Does ‘supra-personal’ moral status — a level above ordinary persons — make sense?

Discussion: Which grounding capacity should set the threshold, and what follows for beings above or below it?

params.text:

Committees and guidelines provide a framework, but the daily reality of ethical research rests on the character of the people involved. W.D. Ross's prima facie obligations — fidelity, reparation, gratitude, beneficence, nonmaleficence — overlap with healthcare virtues such as compassion, discernment, trustworthiness, integrity and conscientiousness.

Discussion: Map these high-level virtues onto concrete choices — designing a trial, obtaining consent, conducting field research. Ethical research is a constant practice that requires a professional character equipped to navigate the grey areas where the rules run out.

params.text:
The pipeline, end to end

You have followed a single logical pipeline. It begins with sanitised, precise linguistic definitions; these let factual data be structured into formally sound arguments; and finally normative frameworks supply the evaluative premise needed to bridge the is–ought gap. Applied consistently, this mechanical approach lets research institutions audit and enforce ethical compliance with transparency — meeting the rigorous standards professional research demands.
Define terms with the right kind of definition; capture both extension and intension; audit out ambiguity (multiple meanings) and vagueness (fuzzy boundaries) before reasoning begins.

Separate premises from conclusions; distinguish validity (structure) from soundness (structure plus true premises); recognise deductive forms; and never try to cross the is–ought gap without an evaluative premise.
Source that evaluative premise from a defensible framework: deontology (duties), utilitarianism (consequences) or virtue ethics (character) — and reason carefully about personhood and moral status.
Stress-test the tools on hard cases, and remember that good intentions are not a safeguard: interrogate your own methods so the pursuit of knowledge never costs human dignity.

params.text: Well done. You now have a working ethical toolbox — a repeatable, transparent method for turning moral questions into disciplined analysis.

Source Materials

This module is based on the following works, as cited on the title slide of the ‘Ethical Analysis Skills and Ethical Toolbox’ deck:

  • Lau, J. Y. F. (2011). An Introduction to Critical Thinking and Creativity: Think More, Think Better. Wiley.
  • Thomson, A. (2002). Critical Reasoning in Ethics: A Practical Introduction. Routledge.
  • Morrow, D. R. (2018). Moral Reasoning: A Text and Reader on Ethics and Contemporary Moral Issues. Oxford University Press.
  • Arnold, N. S. et al. (2014). Philosophy: Traditional and Experimental Readings. Oxford University Press.
  • Loue, S. (2002). Textbook of Research Ethics: Theory and Practice. Kluwer/Springer.
  • Socaciu, E. et al. (2018). Etică și integritate academică (Ethics and Academic Integrity). Editura Universității din București.

Key Concepts & Thinkers Referenced

  • Peter Singer — ‘Famine, Affluence, and Morality’ (the drowning-child analogy).
  • Judith Jarvis Thomson — ‘A Defense of Abortion’ (the violinist thought experiment).
  • Immanuel Kant — the Categorical Imperative: universalizability and respect for persons.
  • W. D. Ross — prima facie obligations (fidelity, reparation, gratitude, beneficence, nonmaleficence).
  • Robert Nozick — the Experience Machine.
  • Aristotle — virtue ethics and the Doctrine of the Mean.

Case Study Background

  • Benzyl alcohol and neonatal ‘gasping syndrome’ (US NICUs, early 1980s).
  • The Belfast Project / Boston College oral-history subpoena controversy.
  • Deception and psychological distress in behavioural research ethics.
